articles.title: The Vrykolakiasmenos Gero-Klousteres and the Priest
articles.author: Στυλιανός Βίος
articles.excerpt: Folk tradition from Lithi, Chios: Gero-Klousteres becomes a vrykolakiasmenos on the day he dies, blocking the priest on the road to Chora until he hurls him against the monastery limestone.

image.alt: Ο Βρυκολακιασμένος Γερο-Κλουστέρης και ο παπάς στο Λιθί Χίου

content.value: One evening, the priest was heading to Chora. That very day, Gero-Klousteres had died. When the priest reached Troulos (a local place name), he saw the old man standing before him with his stick. The old man would not let the priest pass any further and was creating obstacles in his path.

The priest said to the old man:

— "Come now, Gero-Klousteres — think of all we've eaten and drunk together... let me pass."

The old man let him pass.

As the priest walked on, an hour later the old man kept appearing before him again and again, all the way until the priest reached the Monastery. There, just as he opened the monastery gate, the vrykolakiasmenos struck him and hurled him against the limestone wall.

The monks came outside, washed the priest, and he continued on his way to Chora. As he turned to look behind him, a great crowd of vrykolakes suddenly gathered and began throwing stones at him, but not a single stone came close.

articles.author: Στυλιανός Βίος

articles.title: The Pentacle as a Protection Against Becoming a Vrykolakas
articles.author: Στυλιανός Βίος
articles.excerpt: A tradition from Kardamyla, Chios about the use of the pentalf placed in the mouth of the deceased as a protection against becoming a vrykolakas.

image.alt: Tradition about vrykolakes in Kardamyla, Chios

content.value: In those days, the dead would become vourvoulakoi because they did not place the pentalf in their mouths, the priests did not read the proper prayers over them, and they were not kept watch over through the night. A newlywed woman — her husband had died and she was young and frightened — left him alone. The corpse disappeared, and every evening it would come to stand outside the house holding a lit torch in its hand. The priest went and read prayers over it at the grave, and from that time it was never seen again.
According to Anna Vios, aged 90, from Kardamyla.

articles.title: The Vourvoulakoi and the Keyholes - Chios
articles.author: Στυλιανός Βίος
articles.excerpt: A tradition from Chios about vourvoulakoi who enter houses through keyholes, and about an excommunicated man who was exhumed swollen, stood upright in church, and turned to ash the moment he was forgiven.

image.alt: Tradition about vourvoulakoi and keyholes in Chios

content.value: The dead are kept watch over at night so that a cat does not pass over them, because this causes them to become vourvoulakoi and wander at night in their burial shrouds. They return to the house where they died and enter through the keyhole. For this reason, Palm Sunday crosses are placed behind the keyholes.

The excommunicated, first of all, swell up inside their graves, and then they become vourvoulakoi and come out. An excommunicated man was exhumed and found greatly swollen. They brought him to the church and stood him upright. All the people forgave him, and they brought the Bishop who read prayers over him — and immediately he collapsed all at once, falling in a heap to the ground and turning to ash.
According to Marou Stamoulis, aged 60, from Kalamoti.

articles.title: The Vroukolakes of Neapoli, Kozani
articles.author: Σπύρος Συγκολλίτου
articles.excerpt: An extensive account from Anasilitsa (Neapoli, Kozani) about vroukolakes: causes, signs, purification rituals with boiling wine and needles, their dance at crossroads, and the burning ritual performed at the grave on three consecutive Saturdays.

content.value: If anyone passes near the graves, at whatever hour it may be, they stop and make the sign of the cross. They do the same when they pass the place where someone was killed.
At that place they always put some kind of marker to show that blood was shed there — either a wooden cross or a small pile of stones.
They believe that the blood of the murdered man speaks at night. For forty days, those who pass the place of the killing hear the sounds the blood makes: "Oui, oui!"
They tell the family of the murdered man, who then fetch the priest and go to perform the memorial rite. After the reading, the sounds are never heard again.

They always have great fear that the murdered man, with his wounds, will become a vroukolakas. They also fear those whose bodies developed sores from lying motionless through a long illness. All such persons are washed with hot water and scalded with boiling wine, a needle being pushed deep into the wounds.
In this way they open holes in the body so that all impurity may drain out and the dead man will not swell while he still lies in the house. If this is not done, vroukolakes will emerge.
The vroukolakes always take the form of animals, most often a cat, emitting fire from their hindquarters.
They wander the roads, especially at crossroads — where many roads meet — dancing and singing:

If you burned us, what have you done to us?
You didn't stick the torch up our backsides.

They also go into houses, descending through the chimney. There they cause much damage: eating various foods — honey, sweets, fats, lard, butter, and so on — defiling the flour, spilling the grape-must syrup. Sometimes they bang on the windows, and other times they throw stones from the chimney in front of the fire.

As soon as people learn that someone has become a vroukolakas, they do not tell the house where he lived, but go to the grave, light a torch and thrust it into the hole near the head — the opening through which the vroukolakas comes out at night. This is called the burning. It must be done on three consecutive Saturdays, very early, at the breaking of dawn. During the burning, no incense is used. It is always performed at the waning of the moon. They also believe that a vroukolakas will emerge if the body is not watched over the night it lies in the house and a cat or mouse steps over it.

articles.title: Ritual to Prevent Becoming a Vrykolakas - Drosopigi, Arta
articles.author: Ε. Στούμπας
articles.excerpt: A record from Drosopigi, Arta of the ritual in which the priest goes in silence to administer Holy Communion to the dying — because if the dying person does not receive Communion, it is believed they will become a vrykolakas.

content.value: The priest, accompanied by a child who follows holding a kandili — which has rather the shape of a lantern and burns oil within it — goes to the home of the dying person and administers Holy Communion.

During the journey from the church to the house, the priest goes bareheaded, wearing his epitrachelion (stole), and it is forbidden for him to exchange greetings or any other words with those he meets along the way. If the dying person does not receive Holy Communion, it is believed that they will become a vrykolakas.

articles.author: Titos Giohalas
articles.excerpt: A tradition from Evangelismos, Euboea: a vrykolakas (called LJUGAT in Arvanitika) was seen glowing at night near the village. A priest would go to the grave, read prayers, and drive a black-handled knife into the earth.

image.alt: Image related to the vrykolakas in Evangelismos, Euboea

content.value: My mother and grandmother said that if a man died who had not been a good person and the priests had not properly read the funeral rites, he could become a vrykolakas (they called it LJUGAT). This vrykolakas, they say, was seen at night glowing — either near Agios Ioannis, or near the Pournaria, or at Milza. You would look in that direction… and then it vanished.

We believed then that the dead man had become a vrykolakas, and a priest had to be brought to re-read prayers over the grave. The priest went to the tomb, read the prayers, and then drove a black-handled knife into the grave.

articles.title: Kallianoi, Euboea – Destroying the Vrykolakas
articles.author: Titos Giohalas
articles.excerpt: A folk account from Kallianoi, Euboea: a ljugat (vrykolakas) brought human liver to his family each night. He was destroyed only after vinegar was poured into the hole in his grave.

image.alt: Image related to the vrykolakas in Kallianoi, Euboea

content.value: Translation from Arvanitika

My mother told me that there was once a ljugatis (vrykolakas) who appeared every evening. He would bring human liver with him and eat it. When people realized he had become a vrykolakas, they went to his grave and found a hole. They poured a little vinegar into the hole and from that day on he never appeared again. The vinegar made him vanish.
Same story in Greek

The ljugatis — that is, the vrykolakas — used to go to his family and bring them liver from the dead. This happened often, and they would eat it. At some point the family began to suspect something and wondered: «Where does he keep finding all this liver?» They went to his grave and saw there was a hole. That was how he came out, brought the liver, and then returned. They took some vinegar and poured it into the hole. From that moment the vrykolakas never appeared again. This story was told to me by my mother.

articles.title: Hydra – Burial Customs Against Becoming a Vrykolakas
articles.excerpt: Apotropaic burial customs from Hydra: the deceased must never be left alone, water and a candle are placed in the room for three days, and if a cat passes over the body the dead will irrevocably become a vrykolakas.

content.value: According to custom, the deceased must remain one night in his home (with rare exceptions). It is strictly forbidden to leave the body alone in the room at any hour, as this risks the dead becoming a vrykolakas.

In the room of death a vessel of water is placed and the candle that was lit at the moment of death is kept burning. This remains for three days and nights so that «the soul may be refreshed». The doors are locked carefully so that no cat or dog may drink from the water.
If a cat passes over the body, the deceased irrevocably becomes a vrykolakas according to tradition.

articles.title: Ypati, Fthiotida – The Vrykolakas of Fthiotida, 1850
articles.excerpt: A historical account by Dimitris Ainian, fighter of the 1821 Revolution: the deputy mayor of a village in Fthiotida recounts how they exhumed and burned a vrykolakas in 1850, and the narrator offers a rational explanation for the phenomenon.

content.value: As recounted by Dimitris Ainian, fighter of the 1821 War of Independence and first biographer of Karaiskakis. The village deputy mayor of a village in Fthiotida tells him the story in 1850.

During a tour of the region, I arrived very late at the village... and since there was no inn, I turned to the village president for lodging. The president, judging by our appearance that we were not people who would be a burden to whoever hosted us — but rather that he might benefit from our company — offered us a room in his house, so that he could share the billeting schedule with us rather than with the passing soldiers chasing bandits.
Knowing there was no inn, we had already provided all the necessary provisions for that evening; but the president insisted on contributing so that we might pass that night pleasantly.

Later, during various conversations after dinner, the president told us: «If you do not intend to leave very early in the morning, you might witness a most curious spectacle. Six months ago one of our villagers died — a man who, it seems, was not of good character — and he has become a vrykolakas. Tomorrow we plan to exhume him and burn him.»
— And how do you know he became a vrykolakas? (I asked him)

— We see, he said, a fire emerging from his grave every night, moving now in one direction and now in another. You may not believe such things; but we who have seen it with our own eyes cannot doubt it. Two years ago a similar thing happened. Another villager became a vrykolakas, fire appeared at his grave, and many times he went to his house, knocked, disturbed the belongings, and his poor wife nearly died of fear, since none of the neighbours dared accompany her. As soon as evening fell, we all locked our doors and windows and took great care lest the vrykolakas come to our own houses as well.

At last, unable to bear this miserable state of affairs, we decided to open the grave — and what did we find? The body intact, exactly as we had buried it, and indeed fatter and more swollen. We all marvelled when we saw it. Then the priest told us to bring a crowbar; and once it was brought, he said: «Let one of you take the crowbar and, holding it with both hands, strike the body with all your strength at the level of the heart, so that the bar passes through to the other side.»
None of us dared take the crowbar and perform this act.

Then the priest, addressing a young man who appeared thoughtful and timid, said: «Do not be afraid, my child; it is a shame for a man like you to fear a dead body. Do you not know that today is Saturday and a vrykolakas can do no harm today?»

The young man, moved partly by shame and partly by respect for the priest, dared not refuse. He took the crowbar, stood over the body of the vrykolakas, and struck hard at the heart. But what horror we witnessed! The crowbar did not drive into the body, and the vrykolakas recoiled as if alive! I still remember it as if it were happening today. The crowbar fell from our neighbour's hands, and we all nearly fled in panic had the priest not encouraged us, saying that on Saturday a vrykolakas can do no harm. He gave us instructions; we gathered wood, lit a fire upon the body, and after three hours we managed to burn it completely. From that moment we saw nothing further in our village — until this new vrykolakas appeared, whom we intend to exhume and burn as well. But you do not believe in such things.
— And you, Mr Deputy Mayor, do you believe all this and fear it? they asked him.
— Of course I believe it, for I saw it with my own eyes, he answered.
— I can well believe that you saw something, they said, but it is not what it appeared to you, and it has neither the agency nor the power you attribute to it.
— You know a great deal, replied the deputy mayor, but however much you know, how can you persuade me that a vrykolakas does not exist, when I see the fire emerging from the grave?

— The fire, I answered, is a natural phenomenon. It emerges from graves in cemeteries, appears on plains where battles were fought and many fell, in places where executions are carried out and many are buried together, and even in marshy areas. Before such phenomena were explained, many people were terrified by them. For they say that if one ran, the fire would follow; if one turned against it, it would retreat — yet could never be caught.

It is said that Charles IX, King of France, while hunting with others in a forest of Normandy, saw a fiery apparition. All around him fled in terror, leaving him alone. He drew his sword and charged at it, but the apparition cried out to him:
«Flee and do not pursue me!»

But there was one of the most famous physicians in England who understood better what these phenomena were. He made great efforts to capture one of these apparitions and managed to approach it close enough to knock it to the ground. But once it fell, nothing remained but a little viscous substance.

— I confess, said the deputy mayor, that I have neither the courage of Charles nor the boldness of the physician. If I found myself in a similar situation, I would take to my heels; and if I saw the apparition following me, I would faint from fear.
— But if you were to be assured, they told him, that it is simply a natural phenomenon which can do neither harm nor good, you would no longer have the same fear.
— But how could you convince me? says the deputy mayor.

— By explaining the causes of the phenomenon as best I can, I answered. The apparition we see is phosphoric matter, which in summer and towards autumn the sun draws during the day from the decomposition of corpses and from marshes, and which condenses in the night dew. It has the property of igniting upon contact with the atmosphere — and this is the fire we see.
— But how does it move, how does it chase people who flee, and how does it flee from those who pursue it? says the deputy mayor.

— What might seem a strange caprice has a very simple explanation. The phenomenon occurs in complete calm and hovers in the air above the ground. If a light breeze blows, it moves it in another direction. When someone, like Charles, approaches to pursue it, as he moves toward it he pushes the air; and the air pushes the fiery apparition — the faster one pursues it, the faster it retreats. If a man turns to flee, leaving empty space behind him, the air nearby — where the apparition also is — rushes in to fill the void; and since the flight continues, so does the apparition's pursuit, the cause persisting. The moment the runner stops, the air movement ceases; and then the apparition too comes to rest.

— To all this, says the deputy mayor, I know not what to reply, though my mind can scarcely take it in; at any rate I would not dare conduct such an experiment. But regarding the body, which I saw with my own eyes to be almost like a living person and which moved when struck with the bar — what can you say?
— You all went there, I answered, prejudiced by fear; and who can trust your testimony?

— Nevertheless, here is what one may conclude. The young man with the crowbar may have struck hard in his fear; it is possible the body shifted somewhat in decomposition — which happens often. Whatever occurred when it was struck, that motion is not the motion of a living being, but like when you press a lifeless object at one end and it appears to move at the other.

— But how do you explain the vrykolakas passing from house to house, the knocking, the disturbance of things, the untying of animals from the ropes with which they are bound at night — found loose in the morning — and other such occurrences? (said the president)

— These, I told him, are the work not of the dead but of the living, who take advantage of the people's fear and superstition to do all this with impunity and without risk — either to serve some dishonest purpose, or to amuse themselves with their friends by recounting how much terror they caused their cowardly and superstitious neighbours. In proof of this I can assure you with an incident that happened to me personally. Some young men had spread the word that a villager had become a vrykolakas, and that he had been seen in the cemetery moving toward the village as a ball of fire, as such things are said to do. Many inhabitants saw this fire and were so frightened that many would no longer leave their houses for any reason, however urgent.

Since for villagers such a paralysis is harmful, many were preparing the means you are about to use to be rid of the vrykolakas. But I, knowing that the dead do no harm, was wondering what the real cause of this rumour might be; and since I learned that at the same time several thefts of animals, produce and foodstuffs had occurred, I concluded that the evil must be fought elsewhere. I therefore proposed to the villagers that all arm themselves, divide into groups at the highest positions in the village from which the fire had been seen approaching, and keep careful watch — so that if the fire were seen coming toward the village, they would fire upon it. I myself stood at the most critical position. We kept watch all night — nothing appeared; and the same on many nights following. Thus the vrykolakas vanished by this measure alone.

And what did I learn afterwards? Two or three young men of the village had spread and sustained the idea in order to have time to steal their neighbours' produce; and they themselves had made the fire, to lend full credibility to the existence of the vrykolakas.

— This last observation, says the deputy mayor, convinces me more than the previous ones, for here too, since the vrykolakas appeared, there have been quite a few thefts — so much so that I am now tempted to prefer the method of keeping watch for vrykolakes, which you yourself used so successfully.

— That is what I advise you too: to continue or to cease believing that the dead can return; for this contradicts our own religion and it is impossible that they could be destroyed by such ridiculous means as staking and burning.

articles.title: Naxos – Vrykolakes in 1874
articles.excerpt: An account by Nikolaos Dragoumis from 19th-century Naxos: amid plague rumours, a miller's daughters are terrorised nightly by vrykolakes, a man shoots his own cat believing it a demon, and a pious church official returns from the dead.

content.value: The rumour of plague, which in earlier times rarely visited the Peloponnese and the Aegean, had begun to circulate intensely among the people. It was known to all…
And since human life is made of a mixture of happiness and misfortune, grief and laughter, this epidemic was accompanied by a peculiarly comic episode…

The miller who lived next door to me had two daughters who recounted with horror every morning how two vourkólakes had burst in noisily, overturned the furniture, and fled only at the cock's crow. One night he fired at a vrykolakas wandering around his kitchen. In the morning he found his beloved cat dead: «I then saw one of the vourkólakes»…
A Protosynkellos known for his piety was transported to the heavens but returned as a vourkólakas: «Forming an innumerable phalanx, they roamed about…»

articles.title: The Vourvoulakas with the Sieve – Tinos
articles.author: Nikolaos G. Politis
articles.excerpt: A folk tale from the village of Birdemianon, Tinos: an old woman brings a log indoors from the well, which transforms into a vourvoulakas demanding a sieve full of beans. On the feast of the Holy Cross the villagers try to burn it, but it escapes.

content.value: In the village of Birdemianon on Tinos there lived an old woman who had a neighbour living right next door to her.

One night, around midnight, the old woman got up to go and knead bread at the communal oven — for in those days they baked at the village's shared oven. The moment the neighbour saw her, he transformed into a vourvoulakas (vrykolakas) and followed her, frightening her terribly. In the meantime, the woman's husband was returning from the countryside. As he came back, he found a log at the well beneath their house. He tied it with the well rope and hauled it up.
The moment he brought it inside, the log transformed into a vourvoulakas and began shouting at the old woman to bring him a sieve full of beans. She was so terrified she could only watch.
On the feast of the Holy Cross (14 September) they lit a fire to burn him, but the vourvoulakas pulled the rope and vanished before their eyes.

articles.title: Vourvoulakoi – Mykonos
articles.author: Nikolaos G. Politis
articles.excerpt: A folk account from Mykonos: the vourvoulakoi are the restless souls of great sinners who rise from their graves. Relatives protect themselves with a pentagram and rebury them on the islet of Mpáou — but some still manage to return.

content.value: Those who had committed many sins while alive found no rest in death. Instead, they rose from the grave and wandered the places where they had lived. They troubled their families and neighbours, tormenting or killing them.

One was seen riding his horse and going to his field as though he had never died. Another was found every evening sleeping in his own bed. A third knocked on his wife's door at night, demanding entrance.

To protect themselves from the vourvoulakoi (the returning dead), many people, before going to bed at night, used to draw a pentagram on the door with chalk. Others placed a sieve by the door, since it is believed that the vourvoulakas must count all the holes in the sieve before he can enter — and by the time he finishes, morning arrives and he must return to his grave.

Sometimes the dead man's relatives, if he had become a vourvoulakas, were compelled to exhume him. They would take him to be reburied on the islet of Mpáou, since it was believed that there — being cut off from all land — he could no longer trouble anyone.

Yet there were cases where the vourvoulakoi managed to return even from there. Then the relatives had to take them still further away. One was reportedly taken so far out to sea that he was never seen again.

articles.title: The Katachanades of Kalathas – Chania, Crete
articles.author: Nikolaos G. Politis
articles.excerpt: A folk tradition from the Akrotiri peninsula, Chania: priests who did not perform the burial rites correctly caused the dead to become katachanades. A monk eventually banished them all to the small islet of Kalathas.

content.value: In those times, the priests did not know how to bury the dead properly — that is, without performing all the necessary prayers and rites. As a result, many of the dead became katachanades — meaning they found no rest after death and troubled the living.
The Akrotiri peninsula became filled with katachanades who wandered the houses at night, causing disorder and bringing misfortune.

At some point it happened that a number of bodies were buried in the church of Agia Triada — and for the first time, none of them became katachanades. Word spread, and people began bringing their dead to be buried there from great distances, so that they too might find rest.
In return, the people donated fields, vineyards, and olive groves to the monastery.

Later, one of the monks of the monastery performed special exorcism rites and banished all the katachanades to a small islet called Kalathas, near the northern shore of the Akrotiri. There — but also nearby on land — they still gather to this day.

articles.excerpt: A folk account from Kareas, Attika: a vourdoulakas appeared in the Vathy Rema ravine, making a loud hissing noise that terrified the flocks. A man known as 'light-shadowed' finally confronted and banished it with a stone.

content.value: In the Vathy Rema ravine at Kareas, a vourdoulakas used to appear, making a loud noise — a kind of hissing, as they called it — and the sheep were so frightened that they all huddled together in a tight mass. No one dared to approach it.
After some time, a man named Giorgis Tzanetos who was alafroïskiotos (light-shadowed — meaning he had the gift to see and confront such beings) managed to face it.
The vourdoulakas looked like a bloated wineskin standing upright, and continued hissing.
Without hesitation, Giorgis seized a large stone with his left hand and hurled it at the creature. From that day on, the vourdoulakas never appeared again.

articles.title: Galanis – Exo Chora, Zakynthos
articles.author: Nikolaos G. Politis
articles.excerpt: A folk account from Exo Chora, Zakynthos: the vrykolakas Galanis (also known as Tourlides) appears every night at midnight, tormenting the villagers. Those who reveal his existence suffer his vengeance — one man was blinded.

content.value: In Exo Chora, every night around midnight, Galanis appears — also known as Tourlides — and «crosses» people, meaning he torments them. He is a vrykolakas who gives the villagers no peace.

He had set his sights on one particular villager and gave him no rest; he ruined his life daily. After many such torments, the man said to him: «Why don't you go to your kin, poor wretch, among the dead?» And the vrykolakas replied: «I have no kin there.» Galanis, however, did not want it known that he was wandering about, and every time someone said they had seen him, he would do them harm.
Once, out of fear, a man revealed it to his family — and word got out.

One evening Galanis caught the man at Kamaroti, together with his mare. «Did I not tell you not to betray me? I'll gouge your eye out!» he shouted at him. And as he said it, so it was done: the poor man was left with only one eye.

articles.title: Burial of a Vrykolakas on the Islet of Agios Georgios – Mykonos
articles.author: Nikolaos G. Politis
articles.excerpt: A folk account from Mykonos: a villager found dead in his field rises two days after burial, terrorising the village. After a failed reburial he grows worse — breaking doors, beating people, emptying jars — until he is burned with pitch on the islet of Agios Georgios.

content.value: In the village, a peasant was found dead in his field. They buried him, but two days later he returned from his grave. At night he appeared in the streets and houses, disturbing things, extinguishing lights, and frightening everyone.

At first the villagers paid little attention, but when the situation began to get out of hand, they decided first to observe the ninth-day memorial and then to exhume him. Indeed, ten days later they dug him up, carried him to another spot, and reburied him with all the proper rites.

But he did not rest. On the contrary, things grew even worse. He beat people at night, broke doors and windows, tore their clothes, and emptied their jugs and pitchers. No house in the village was safe.
Finally the villagers decided to take him to the islet of Agios Georgios. There they piled up wood, covered it with pitch, and burned him. From that time on, there was peace at last.

articles.title: The Kouvelos – Milos
articles.author: Nikolaos G. Politis
articles.excerpt: A folk account from Milos: a man named Kouvelos who cursed himself at the moment of death became a vrykolakas. An elder advised exhuming the body, removing the heart, burning it, and scattering the ashes to the four winds.

content.value: When a person is in their death agony, if they curse themselves or an enemy curses them at that very moment, the cursed one, upon dying, becomes a vrykolakas. The earth cannot dissolve his body, and he rises from the grave and wanders the world, causing harm — strangling people or striking them with illness.

The evil does not pass unless, through prayers, the dead man's body dissolves in the grave. A single priest alone has no power in such a case. A bishop must come, perform a concelebration with twelve priests, and recite the appropriate prayers.

A certain Kouvelos, long ago, became a vrykolakas because at the moment of his death he cursed himself. Once dead, Kouvelos wandered the fields and the village day and night, strangling or striking people, until they were dying faster than they could be buried.

Then an elder advised them to exhume Kouvelos's body, split it open, remove his heart, burn it, and scatter its ashes to the four winds. They did as the elder said — and the vrykolakas troubled them no more.

articles.title: The Vourdoulakas – Arachova
articles.author: Nikolaos G. Politis
articles.excerpt: A detailed folk account from Arachova: a man killed and left unburied for a long time becomes a vourdoulakas who steals eggs and milk. A Saturday-born man exhumes and destroys it by piercing its heart and boiling it in vinegar.

content.value: Once, somewhere, a man was killed and lay unburied for a long time. Eventually they found him and buried him in his village. Some time later the villagers noticed that their eggs were disappearing, their milk was going sour, and other strange things were occurring.
One night the priest went to the church and saw a demon emerging from that murdered man's grave and entering people's stables. It went before the widow's house and called out to her.

The priest told all the villagers what he had seen and heard. Then an elder stood up and said: «The demon coming out of the grave is none other than that murdered man who was left unburied for so long — he has become a vourdoulakas.»
The villagers did as the elder told them: they found a Saturday-born man and put the matter to him. He said: «Boil two cauldrons of vinegar, heat an awl in the fire, and have the following ready...»

When they reached the grave, the Saturday-born man first washed his face and hands with vinegar. Then he took his cape and propped it upright against a tree facing the grave, arranging it so it appeared to be a man.

They exhumed the vourdoulakas. He was large, fat, red all over, and with bulging eyes. He turned to the Saturday-born man in fury and said: «Who betrayed me?» «That one there, leaning against the tree,» he replied. The vourdoulakas charged at the cape, and at that moment the Saturday-born man seized him from behind.

Then the Saturday-born man grabbed the vourdoulakas, tore open his chest, pulled out his heart, pierced it with the awl, and threw it into one of the two cauldrons of boiling vinegar. He then poured the vinegar over the body, gathered the bones, and burned everything. From that moment on there was no more trouble.

articles.title: The Katachanas – Kallikratis, Chania
articles.author: Nikolaos G. Politis
articles.excerpt: A detailed folk account from Kallikratis, Chania: a katachanas of unknown origin depopulates the village by killing children and adults. A shepherd — his godfather — shelters in the tomb and witnesses the demon's nocturnal raids, then betrays him to the priests.

content.value: In the old days, in the village of Kallikrati, a katachanas appeared — and no one knew who he had been or where he was from. This katachanas slashed children and many grown men, and laid the village and the surrounding area to waste.
There was a shepherd, a godfather-friend of his, who grazed animals near the church. He was caught by rain and went to the tomb to shelter from it. After that, he decided to sleep and rest there.

That night, as the katachanas wished to set out again to cut down people, he said to the shepherd: «Get up, godfather, leave from here, for I have business and must go.» The shepherd did not answer, nor did he turn to look at him.

For this reason, the fourth time the katachanas addressed him, the shepherd said: «I will not get up from here, for I am afraid, godfather — lest you have something evil in you from a bad wind and harm me. So I will not move until you give me your word that you will cause me no harm.» And the katachanas swore he would not harm his godfather-friend.

He rose from there, took up his weapons, and came out of the tomb. They parted, and the katachanas said to him: «But godfather, do not go away — sit here and wait, for I have business nearby; I will return and we will talk.»
The katachanas went about ten miles away, where there was a blessed couple, and he slashed them; then he came back. His godfather saw him returning carrying a liver, his hands wet with blood.

After that he said: «Let us sit, godfather, and eat.» The shepherd acted as though he was eating, but he ate only dry bread and from that food he ate nothing — instead he hid a piece in his chest. When the time came to part, the katachanas said: «Do not forget, godfather, what you heard and saw tonight — keep it to yourself, for if you betray me, I will do you harm.»

But the shepherd lost no time: he gave word to priests and other men, and they went and found him in the tomb, and recognised all the evil he had done. They burned him. But his godfather did not escape unharmed — when the katachanas was half-burned, he raised himself up to see, and the katachanas spat a great mouthful of blood that struck him in the leg. That leg rotted and the shepherd died not long after.

articles.author: Nikolaos G. Politis

content.value: On Mykonos, on a large sandy beach they call Megali Ammos or Vida, a captain is buried. He died suddenly aboard his ship, which was anchored nearby, and they brought him ashore and buried him there on the beach.

Many have seen him: he is very handsome, young, about twenty-three years old, dressed in fine clothes. Once he chased some passers-by, but could not catch them — he grew tired and stopped. Those he had chased then turned and looked back at him.
On the flat stone where he stands, they say is his stoicheio — his spirit. He is called the Kapetanaki of Megali Ammos.

articles.title: The Varvalákas – Nanou, Symi
articles.author: Nikolaos G. Politis
articles.excerpt: A folk account from Nanou, Symi, in the local dialect: a fisherman named Sotiris encounters a varvalákas (vrykolakas) while fishing. The creature paralyses him until he breaks free by hurling his fishing rod and salt at it.

content.value: Once, Sotiris of Patatoukas went fishing in the sea near Nanou. There he found a fine fishing spot and cast his line. He kept catching one after another.

He drank one down the throat, and kept catching them one by one. His catch was nearly done. He went to get a barnacle for bait, bent down — and just as he bent, he felt something breathing like a human. He looked carefully to see if it might be a person.

And again, just as he straightened up he felt it breathing like a human; but when he bent to look and search — nothing. Then he heard a hair-raising voice from inside the cliff, and then another right behind him. He was seized with fear…

He went to take his fishing rod to leave — it would not come loose. He tried to flee himself — his legs would not move. Finally, after much effort, he grabbed the fishing rod and a piece of salt he had grated, and fled.

articles.title: The Vrykolakiasmeno Child – Dafnos, Fokida
articles.author: Dim. Loukopoulos
articles.excerpt: A folk account from Dafnos (formerly Vostinitsa), Fokida: a stillborn baby becomes a vrykolakas and suckles its mother at night. A visitor discovers it by the weight pressing on his chest, and the family burns and stakes the infant's body.

content.value: In the old days people became vrykolakes because they were not read over properly when they died. The priests did not know their letters and so the dead would rise, as they say.

Once, a woman in Vostinitsa (modern Dafnos) named Chliarina miscarried during labour. The baby came out alive but then died. They wrapped it in blankets and put it in the baby carriage inside the house.
A few days later the child came back to life. (It had become a vrykolakas.) The vrykolakas went and suckled its mother at night, and she fell ill and nearly died, not knowing what was happening.
One evening, Panagiotis from Kostaritsa (Fokida) visited her at her home.
That night he lay down to sleep in the house. He felt an intense pressure on his chest from the vrykolakas, and he threw it away from him, thinking it was a cat or a dog.

All night it did not let him sleep. Then he got up and said: «Get up, sister, and light the fire! Tell me, sister — that child, what did you do with it? Tonight I suffered terribly; the vrykolakas was pressing down on me! Where did you put it?»
The woman answered: «We have it in the little carriage, brother. Come, let us look, for I too have been suffering tonight!»
They got up and looked. The child had blood-red fingernails and its hair had grown long. They took it, burned it in the fire, and must have staked it as well.
The story was told by the author's mother, who was originally from Vostinitsa.

articles.title: The Vrykolakas of Malandrino – Fokida
articles.author: Dim. Loukopoulos
articles.excerpt: A folk account from Malandrino, Fokida: a man who dies far from home becomes a vrykolakas, returning nightly to his wife — combing the children's hair, sitting by her side — until his father-in-law, a priest, places a cross at the door and the family goes to burn the body.

content.value: Once a man from Vostinitsa spent the whole winter with his sheep at Malandrino. There he died and was buried. But he became a vrykolakas and came from Malandrino to Vostinitsa (modern Dafnos) to visit his wife.
He combed the children's hair. He drank and sat beside his wife.
She was too frightened to tell anyone, because the vrykolakas warned her to say nothing. But when he began to make advances to her, she went to her father-in-law and told him what was happening.
Her father-in-law was a priest.
But before going to her father-in-law, the woman asked the vrykolakas husband: «You, my husband — you sold all the rams; what did you do with the money?»
He answered her: «It is in the sheepfold, at the back — go and get it from there.»
As soon as she told her father-in-law, he made a cross and placed it at the door, and said to his daughter-in-law: «I will sleep here too, my child.»
The vrykolakas came to the door, and seeing the cross he said: «Well, what can I do now... Remove that (the cross) so I can come in. What shall I do with you, now that you have betrayed me?»

The next day the old priest took his daughter-in-law and some men and went to Malandrino, to the sheepfold. They dug and found the vrykolakas's money — and found the vrykolakas buried there too. They scalded him with boiling water and burned him, and from that moment he never returned.

articles.title: The Tradition of Vrykolakes in Vourvoura – Arkadia
articles.author: K. I. Mantzourannis
articles.excerpt: A folk account from Vourvoura, Arkadia: if an animal passes over a corpse when it is unguarded, the dead person becomes a vrykolakas. The body exits through a hole in the grave and wanders. As a precaution, cats are bagged and locked away until burial.

content.value: Whenever a person dies, their relatives keep watch over the body — because if, at a moment when no one is nearby, a cat, a dog, a hen, or any other animal passes over it, the deceased becomes a vrykolakas and rises.

A hole forms above the grave. Through this hole the vrykolakas — that is, the dead person — emerges in the form he had while alive. He walks here and there, and often goes to his house and disturbs his family.
To prevent a cat from passing over the body, they are all gathered and put in sacks, which are tied shut until the hour of burial, when they are set free.

articles.title: The Vrykolakiasmeni Panogiannou (c. 1800) – Vourvoura, Arkadia
articles.author: K. I. Mantzourannis
articles.excerpt: A folk account from Vourvoura, Arkadia, c. 1800: Panogiannou, who died unjustly in a house fire, returns as a vrykolakas eating her son's flour at night. Her son eventually shoots her and she is never seen again.

content.value: Panogiannou, who met an unjust end — burned when her house caught fire — became a vrykolakas and went at night to her child's house to eat flour. Others saw her too, as she went to other houses in the neighbourhood.

One of the neighbours saw her and she was coming toward him with her head covered in a cloth of the kind worn in the time of Turkish rule. The son ran, closed the door, and hid in the bed where his brothers and sisters were sleeping.
She came to the door, knocked, and spoke to them. She said: «Open up, my son.»
They recognised her voice but did not open for her, and she vanished.
Another night Pappadogiannou saw her. She had gone to fetch wood outside her yard and saw her standing pressed against the wall. Many others saw her too.
Her son could no longer bear having his flour eaten. One night he hid himself, and when he saw her he shot her. From that moment no one ever saw her again.

articles.title: The Dance of the Vrykolakes at the Church – Vourvoura, Arkadia
articles.author: K. I. Mantzourannis
articles.excerpt: A folk account from Vourvoura, Arkadia: a man who cursed his severed finger causes a demon to enter it and create a vrykolakas. A brave villager joins the vrykolakes' naked dance at the church door, learns where the creature hides, and the village burns it with vinegar and oil.

content.value: Once a man cut his finger. He threw it into the hollow of a plane tree, saying the Devil could have it.

The Devil entered the finger and it became a vrykolakas. At night it turned into a wineskin and rolled down the road. Those who saw it died of fright. People did not know what it was and said it was a spirit (stoicheio).
One evening the men made a wager of 100 grosia — to be won by whoever had the nerve to go at night to the door of the church where the vrykolakes danced. One of them accepted the challenge.
He went and saw them dancing naked. He undressed as well and began dancing with them. They danced and chanted «ntirni-ntirni».
The vrykolakes had no visible genitals. They turned and asked him: «What is that hanging there?» And he answered that he did not know what it was, shrugging his shoulders.

They danced until the first cockerel crowed, and they said: «A white cockerel crows — dance on, let us dance.» The cockerel crowed a second time and they said: «A black cockerel crows — be gone, let us go.»
As they began to part, they asked one another where they were from. One said from Agios Nikolaos, another from the Panagia, and the last said he was from the plane tree of Agios Georgios.

As soon as the man returned, he told his friends that the thing that came out (the wineskin) was in the plane tree. They went there, took out the wineskin, burned it with vinegar and oil — and it never appeared again.

articles.title: 1837 The Katachanades (Vrykolakes) in Crete by Robert Pashley
articles.author: Robert Pashley
articles.excerpt: Robert Pashley's memoirs on the Katachanades (vrykolakes) of Crete. He describes folk beliefs in Askipho and Andropolis, the burning of corpses as a last resort, and the decrease of such phenomena due to increased priestly skill in the 19th century.

image.alt: Engraving of Crete from the 19th century, Pashley era

content.value: When I was at Askipho, I had enquired about the Vrykolakes, or Katachanades as the Cretans call them, of whom I had heard from Manias and other compatriots, and whose existence and evil deeds constitute a common article of popular belief throughout the island.

Naturally, this belief is particularly strong in the mountains. If anyone ventures to question it, undeniable facts are put forward to silence the sceptics. At Andropolis I find myself on ground that has long been haunted by them and is renowned through numerous stories — some of which are quite entertaining — recording their exploits.

When, then, this customary religious ceremony — to which they resort first — proves ineffective, the inhabitants of the area go on Saturday to the tomb, dig up the body and burn it with fire; an act to which the Greeks consent only in absolute necessity, owing to the religious horror they feel at burning a body upon which the Holy Oil has been poured by the priest in performing the last rite of their religion upon the dying.

The Sfakiots also generally believe that the devastations committed by these nocturnal wanderers were, formerly, far more frequent than they are today; and have become comparatively rare, solely owing to the increased zeal and skill now possessed by the members of the priesthood!

articles.title: The Vrykolakes on the Aliakmon River & the Priest's Fine
articles.author: Robert Pashley
articles.excerpt: Historical record by Robert Pashley (1837) about a priest in Larissa who examined two bodies in the Aliakmon River as vrykolakes. The Metropolitan fined him 250 piastres and threatened defrocking for similar actions, restoring peace to the diocese.

image.alt: The Aliakmon river, where bodies were examined as vrykolakes

content.value: The enlightenment of the episcopal order in certain parts of Turkey in our days appears, from the following story, to be greater than that of our own English bishops seven hundred years ago.

Around the beginning of the current century, the Metropolitan of Larissa received information that a priest had exhumed two bodies and thrown them into the Aliakmon, on the pretext that they were Vrykolakes.

When summoned before the bishop, the priest confessed the act and, as justification, claimed that rumour had it that a large animal, accompanied by flames, had been seen emerging from the tomb where the two bodies had been buried.

The bishop began by compelling the priest to pay him two hundred and fifty piastres (his Holiness did not mention that he distributed the money to the poor). He then published throughout the diocese that every similar offence would be punished with double the fine and certain defrocking, and thus effectively brought peace to all the vrykolakes of his episcopal province.

articles.title: Sophronios and the Spectral Entity of Milos
articles.author: Rodd Rennell
articles.excerpt: The story of Sophronios about a spectral entity on Milos. An excommunicated man's body was found intact, with veins full of blood. Monks of St Basil planned to boil it in wine, but decomposition occurred simultaneously with the Patriarch lifting the excommunication.

image.alt: Byzantine church on Milos, where the incident with the spectral body took place

content.value: A story is told by Sir Paul Rycaut, who served for many years as British ambassador to Constantinople and previously as consul at Smyrna, during the second half of the 17th century. His source was a monk named Sophronios, of great repute in Smyrna, who had himself been an eyewitness to what he described, on the island of Milos, where the inhabitants had long been terrified by a dreadful nocturnal spectral presence, supposed to emanate from the tomb of a man who had died excommunicated.

The tomb was opened and the body was found intact, with its veins full of blood. The monks of Saint Basil held a council, and their collective wisdom decided that the proper course of action was to dismember the body and boil it in wine, according to tradition.
The relatives of the deceased, however, managed to delay the execution of this decision and sent representatives to Constantinople to beseech the Patriarch to lift the excommunication.
In the meantime, the body was placed in the church, where services were continually held for the repose of the soul.

One day, while Sophronios himself was performing the rites, a loud cracking sound was suddenly heard from the coffin. It was opened, and they found that the body had entirely decomposed, as if the person had been dead for seven years.

The hour of the event was carefully recorded, and when the delegation returned from Constantinople it was found to coincide exactly with the moment at which the Patriarch had lifted the condemnation of the deceased.

content.value: In Rhodes the vrykolakas is called a 'katachanas'; in Mytilene, 'vrokolako'. There is no more immediate or effectual way to rid yourself of a troublesome or tiresome Mytilinian than to say to him: 'Off with you — may the vrykolakas take you.' articles.title: The Old Woman Vrykolakas in Tsepelovo
articles.author: G. K. Kavvadias
articles.excerpt: Folkloric narrative from Tsepelovo, Ioannina: an old woman becomes a vrykolakas after death on account of her bad life, and eats with the dogs. Her relatives exorcise her with a doxology and acts of charity.

content.value: And can a human being also become a spirit — and an evil one at that? Of course it can. Especially if one has not lived a good life. Then one becomes a vrykolakas, tormenting both oneself and the living. An old woman told us the following 'true' story.

An old woman would not give her leftover food to people, but threw it to the dogs instead. Three days after her death, her daughter-in-law saw her come back and eat at night with the dogs. She ran immediately to her husband and told him.

He thought she was saying it out of the animosity that usually exists between a mother-in-law and a daughter-in-law. But she persisted. So the following night they both kept watch and truly saw the old woman eating with the dogs. To be rid of the vrykolakas, they both ran to the priest and had a doxology performed.
And to make amends for the injustice the old woman had done while alive, they hastened to distribute gifts in her name to the poor. And the old woman was never seen again!

content.value: When the sick person breathes his last, they change his clothes and lay the deceased in the centre of the room on a new sheet and rug, with his hands bound in a cross and likewise his head and feet.
He is placed facing East and adorned with flowers. These same flowers and a little soil will fill the pillow placed with him in the grave.
At the spot where he died they drive in a nail, and for three nights they continually light a candle and cense the room three times.
If the deceased is kept at home during the night, millet is scattered around him on the mattress and no cat is allowed into the room to jump over him — for then he would become a vrykolakas.
A coin is placed in the deceased's mouth, and a wax cross is fashioned over his mouth and forehead.
If the deceased's eyes are open, it is said that he caught sight of a distant relative. And if the deceased is handsome, it is said that he will take another with him.

articles.title: The Dentedes of Isaakio
articles.excerpt: Collected description of the dentedes (vrykolakes) of Isaakio, with three stories of dead husbands returning and the methods used to destroy them.

content.value: The tradition comes from villages of Eastern Thrace. When a dead person became a vrykolakas, he would come at night and walk about — a thing like a heap, like a beehive — and roam the roads and houses. There where we sat in the evening we saw a thing like a black heap walking.

We did not bother them and they did not bother us; they would get up and leave and we were not afraid of them. Our grandmother used to tell us that these were bewitched souls from our kin who came to see us — if we did not bother them, they did not bother us.
It was not good when a dead man became a dentes. He would come out of the grave at night fully alive and go home. Only his nose was rather snub.

I remember how people discussed with tears over in our village three dentedes who returned to their homes — and all three had been married. One who went home the first night was seen by his wife fully alive and she was frightened. 'Do not be frightened,' he told her, 'wife, it is I, your husband. Since I died I have become a dentes. They did not accept me in the other world, and so every night I shall come and see you.'

After this happened once or twice, the wife told her mother. 'Mother, such and such a thing — he comes every night to the house. What am I to do? I am afraid. A cold and terrible thing.' Her mother, who knew about these matters, told her: 'One night, daughter, ask him where he hides in the daytime.' And one night she asked him, and he told her he hid in the hollow of an elm tree on the outskirts of the village.
Early in the morning she told her mother, and they gathered others and went and poured kerosene into the hollow and set it alight. The dentes inside howled like an ox — and was never seen again.

Another time, again, a dentes appeared to his wife and came all night, ate and drank, and stayed with her until dawn. They told her too to ask where he stayed in the daytime, and he told her in the chicken coop. The next day they burned the chicken coop, and the dentes inside exploded — and was never seen again.

To the third wife whose dead husband appeared as a dentes, he lay with her at night and the woman became pregnant. The child that was born had a snub nose just like its father. He would not say where he hid in the daytime and they could not burn him.

The woman's whole family knew but did not know what to do. Someone advised them. One night the wife put oil in a frying pan and heated it, pretending she was going to fry eggs for them to eat. At that moment the dentes arrived at the house and went to see what his wife was frying so he could eat.

The woman then seized the pan with the boiling oil and struck him full in the face, burning him with it. His face was burned and he could not see. He screamed with pain, flew into a rage, and began to chase his wife to catch her, threatening to strangle her if he caught her for the harm she had done him, and blindly trying to seize her.

His wife opened the window and jumped out to escape. Her screaming woke their baby, who was sleeping in the cradle and began to cry in fright. He heard it crying, and in his rage at not being able to strangle his wife, he strangled his own child. From then on he vanished and was never seen again.

articles.title: The Vourvoulakoi of Tholopotami, Chios
articles.author: Stylianos Vios
articles.excerpt: Folk tradition from Tholopotami, Chios, about vourvoulakoi who danced at midnight at the Leivadi to the music of a mysterious finger, and vanished once the finger was found and buried.

content.value: In the old days vourvoulakoi would come into the village, and people would shut themselves in their houses early.
At midnight the vourvoulakoi would start their dance at the Leivadi, and a finger would play music.
One curious and fearless man stayed in the Leivadi to see what the vourvoulakoi would do.
When midnight had passed they scattered one by one, and their leader was a sack.
He followed it until it went outside the village and the sack entered a pile of gravel.
In the morning he took men with him and they went and dug and found a human finger.
They took it to the cemetery and buried it. From then on the vourvoulakoi disappeared.
According to Pantelis Ntoulis of Tholopotami, aged 77.

articles.title: The Vourvoulakoi of Lithi, Chios
articles.author: Stylianos Vios
articles.excerpt: Folk tradition from Lithi, Chios, about vourvoulakoi — undead figures who came down from the cemetery and were dispersed by a priest.

image.alt: The Vourvoulakoi of Lithi, Chios

content.value: In the old days the priests did not know how to read the burial rites properly, they did not put a cross in the dead man's mouth, and so the evil entered them and they became vourvoulakoi. The vourvoulakoi would then come down from the cemetery rolling a sack.
A priest went to hold a service and saw them rolling the sack and dancing and singing and everything.
The vourvoulakoi came down from the cemetery, rolling a sack, dancing and singing in the night, causing fear among the inhabitants of the village.
"Your little black fez — tira mola — I shall make it"
And the priest said to them three times:
"Shame on your beards and your pendants!"
And they vanished from before him at once.
According to Michail Klosteridis of Lithi, aged 50.

sources.name: Chian Traditions — Folklore Bulletin of the Hellenic Folklore Society, Vol. IX
